title: Sum of even numbers
prompt: Read one line of integers separated by spaces. Print the sum of the even numbers only.
starter:
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Print the sum of the even numbers
solution:
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()))
print(sum(n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0))
explanation: A number is even when n % 2 == 0. Filter the list with that condition and add up what is left.

title: Count the vowels
prompt: Read one line of text. Print how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) it contains, counting upper and lower case.
starter:
text = input()

# Print the number of vowels
solution:
text = input()
print(sum(1 for ch in text.lower() if ch in "aeiou"))
explanation: Convert the text to lower case first so one membership test against "aeiou" covers both cases.

title: Palindrome check
prompt: Read one line of text. Ignoring spaces, punctuation and letter case, print YES if it reads the same backward as forward, otherwise NO.
example_in: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
starter:
text = input()

# Print YES or NO
solution:
text = input()
clean = [ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalnum()]
print("YES" if clean == clean[::-1] else "NO")
explanation: Keep only letters and digits in lower case, then compare the sequence with its reverse (slice [::-1]).

tests.stdin: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

title: Nth Fibonacci number
prompt: Read an integer n (0 or greater). Print the nth Fibonacci number, where F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1.
starter:
n = int(input())

# Print the nth Fibonacci number
solution:
n = int(input())
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
    a, b = b, a + b
print(a)
explanation: Iterating with two variables runs in O(n) time. The naive recursive version repeats work and takes exponential time.

title: Binary search
prompt: The first line holds sorted integers separated by spaces. The second line holds a target. Print the zero-based index of the target, or -1 if it is absent. Use binary search.
starter:
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
target = int(input())

low, high = 0, len(values) - 1
# Halve the search range until the target is found
solution:
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
target = int(input())
low, high = 0, len(values) - 1
answer = -1
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if values[mid] == target:
        answer = mid
        break
    if values[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
print(answer)
explanation: Each comparison discards half of the remaining range, so the search takes O(log n) steps instead of O(n).

title: Round-robin scheduling
prompt: The first line is the time quantum. The second line lists the burst times of processes P1, P2, ... in arrival order (all arrive at time 0). Simulate round-robin scheduling and print the order in which the processes finish, separated by spaces.
starter:
from collections import deque

quantum = int(input())
bursts = list(map(int, input().split()))
queue = deque((f"P{i + 1}", burst) for i, burst in enumerate(bursts))
finished = []

# Run each process for one quantum, then move it to the back if it is not done
solution:
from collections import deque

quantum = int(input())
bursts = list(map(int, input().split()))
queue = deque((f"P{i + 1}", burst) for i, burst in enumerate(bursts))
finished = []
while queue:
    name, remaining = queue.popleft()
    remaining -= quantum
    if remaining > 0:
        queue.append((name, remaining))
    else:
        finished.append(name)
print(" ".join(finished))
explanation: Round robin takes the process at the front of the ready queue, runs it for one time slice, and sends it to the back if it still has work left.

title: Greatest common divisor
prompt: Read two positive integers on one line. Print their greatest common divisor using the Euclidean algorithm.
starter:
a, b = map(int, input().split())

# Repeat: replace (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is 0
solution:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
while b:
    a, b = b, a % b
print(a)
explanation: The Euclidean algorithm relies on gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b). When the remainder reaches 0, the other value is the answer.

title: Filter and sort
prompt: List the name and salary of every employee who earns more than 6000, highest salary first.
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM Employee WHERE salary > 6000 ORDER BY salary DESC
explanation: WHERE keeps the rows that meet the condition and ORDER BY ... DESC sorts them from highest to lowest.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)

title: Average salary per department
prompt: For each department_id that is not NULL, show the department_id and the average salary of its employees.
solution: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM Employee WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY department_id
explanation: GROUP BY forms one group per department and AVG is computed for each group. NULL must be tested with IS NOT NULL, not with <>.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)

title: Join two tables
prompt: Show each employee name with the name of their department. Leave out employees who have no department.
solution: SELECT e.name, d.name FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
explanation: An inner join returns only the rows that match in both tables, so the employee without a department is excluded.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)

title: Departments with several employees
prompt: Show the department name and the number of employees for departments that have at least 2 employees.
solution: SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) FROM Department d JOIN Employee e ON e.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups afterwards, so conditions on COUNT(*) belong in HAVING.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)

title: Above-average earners
prompt: List the names of employees whose salary is higher than the average salary of all employees.
solution: SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee)
explanation: The subquery computes one value, the overall average, and the outer query compares each row with it.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)

title: Departments without employees
prompt: List the names of departments that have no employees.
solution: SELECT d.name FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL
explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every department. Where no employee matches, the employee columns are NULL, which the WHERE clause selects. NOT EXISTS works too.
schema:
Department(department_id, name, location)
Employee(employee_id, name, salary, hire_year, department_id)
